    Returns
    -------
    PaperSubset
        What was written.

    Raises
    ------
    NotAStoreError
        If ``source`` is not a paper store, or ``store`` not a store with a build.
    StoreBuildError
        If ``root`` may not take the subset (see :func:`labdata.store.subset.check_new_root`).
    LabdataError
        If the source is saving its tables, a table changes during the read, or a ``files``
        row names a file the source does not hold. Run it again once the source's pass ends.
    """
    read_toml_marker(source, MARKER, "a paper store")
    opened = open_store(store)
    build = named_build(opened.root, opened.settings)
    check_new_root(root, source, MARKER, build.name, "paper store")

    before = _stamps(source)
    keys = _linked(source, build)
    rows = {table.name: _rows(source, table, keys) for table in tables.TABLES}
    read_at = utc_stamp()
    _unchanged(source, before)
    for row in rows[tables.ATTEMPTS.name]:
        row["account"] = None

    root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    marker = root / MARKER
    if not marker.is_file():
        lines = [
            toml_line("format_version", FORMAT_VERSION),
            toml_line(SUBSET_OF_KEY, build.name),
            toml_line(COPY_TO_KEY, ""),
            toml_line("drive_remote", ""),
            toml_line("drive_folder", ""),
        ]
        write_atomic(marker, "\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    named = sorted({f["path"] for f in rows[tables.FILES.name] if f["path"]})
    for rel in named:
        _copy_file(source, root, rel)
    _unchanged(source, before)
    written = [tables.write(root, table, rows[table.name]) for table in tables.TABLES]
    _drop_unnamed(root, set(named))
    readme = paths.README.at(root)
    write_atomic(readme, _readme(source, build.name, read_at))
    kept = {r["paper"] for r in rows[tables.PAPERS.name]}
    return PaperSubset(
        root=root,
        papers=len(kept),
        files=len(named),
        bytes=sum(p.stat().st_size for p in (*written, *(root / n for n in named), marker, readme)),
    )

items.title: Run the paper store
items.text:
The paper store sits beside the GEO/SRA store. It holds the papers that the store's Series and BioProjects link to, and the status of each one. One long-running Slurm job, the paper job, keeps it current. Each day it fetches what it can, and once a month it takes in new papers.

Google Cloud Storage (GCS) holds the paper store, and the paper job changes it on a work disk on the cluster. Each pass goes through the same steps as a GEO/SRA store update:

  1. Restore, by hand and only when the work disk is empty or behind GCS. See Restore the store from GCS.
  2. Check that the work disk is in step with GCS.
  3. Update: the daily pass or the PMC sync changes the work disk.
  4. Finalize: copy the changes to GCS. A pass is done only once GCS holds it.

items.title: Set up once
items.text:
The paper store reads the GEO/SRA store that LABDATA_STORE names, or else the one labdata store configure saved. Make sure one of them is set, then make the paper store:

labdata papers init /path/to/paper-store \
  --copy-to gcs:<gcs-bucket>/datalake/paper-store

Save your logins. The NCBI one fetches PubMed records. The OpenAlex accounts buy paper copies, 100 a day each:

labdata ncbi configure
labdata papers configure

labdata papers configure asks for one email and API key per account. Leave the email blank to finish. Without accounts, the daily pass skips OpenAlex and says so. A running job reads the accounts at each pass, so new ones count from the next pass, with no restart.

For the copy to Google Cloud Storage (GCS), set up the gcs rclone remote and log in as Copy the store to GCS shows. Leave out --copy-to to run with no copy. The job's rclone reads your own config, ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf, even when your shell sets RCLONE_CONFIG; set LABDATA_RCLONE_CONFIG before sbatch to use another file.

items.title: Fill the store the first time
items.text:
The first PMC sync takes in every linked paper, so it runs much longer than a monthly one: plan for most of a day. It stores about half a terabyte, mostly supplementary files and figures, so check the free space first. Submit it once by hand, from the repository folder on the cluster, with more CPUs and a longer time limit:

export LABDATA_PAPERS=/path/to/paper-store
df -h "$LABDATA_PAPERS"
sbatch --job-name=labdata-papers-backfill --partition=cpu_batch \
  --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G --time=2-00:00:00 \
  --output=labdata-papers-backfill.%j.log \
  --wrap "pixi run labdata papers pmc-sync"

If it stops, submit it again. It goes on from where it stopped. The paper job can start at the same time: it waits until the first sync is done.

To fill the store in rounds, add --sample 0.01, then --sample 0.1, then run it with no --sample. Each round skips the papers the last round looked up this month. A sampled sync does not count as the month's PMC sync: paper-status.json records it as the last pass, with its sample share, but only a sync over all papers sets last_pmc_sync_success and last_pmc_sync_build. So the paper job still runs the month's PMC sync after a sampled round.

The first copy to GCS sends all of it, with --full. It uploads every file and deletes nothing in GCS. Run it once by hand, as its own job, after the first sync ends, so the paper job's daily pass does not wait behind it:

sbatch --job-name=labdata-papers-copy --partition=cpu_batch \
  --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=8G --time=1-00:00:00 \
  --output=labdata-papers-copy.%j.log \
  --wrap "pixi run labdata papers copy --full"

Log in to rclone first: the login lasts one day. Later copies send only the files added, changed or deleted since the last copy that worked, so their cost follows the day's changes, not the size of the store. Each copy ends by sending its copy record, a hidden file at the paper store root that lists what GCS holds. Until a full copy has worked once, the job's copies do nothing and the log asks for --full.

items.title: Start the paper job
items.text:
export LABDATA_PAPERS=/path/to/paper-store
sbatch scripts/papers/serve.sbatch

The job asks for 2 CPUs and 8 GB on cpu_batch, for the 14 days that partition allows. It runs the daily pass each day after 00:30 UTC, and the PMC sync on the 3rd of each month. It also runs the PMC sync when a refresh makes a new GEO/SRA build current, so the papers the new build links come in soon after. That sync counts as the month's, so a refresh on the 1st or 2nd leaves no sync for the 3rd. Each pass ends with a copy of its changes to GCS, even a pass that fails. The job never runs a full copy.

PMC gives the article text, figures and supplements, while OpenAlex and host links give a PDF only. So when a paper fetched from OpenAlex or a host link later appears in PMC, the PMC sync takes its PMC files and then deletes the old PDF.

At start, the job makes sure two more jobs wait behind it. When the running job ends, the next one takes over; if that one fails at start, the one after it takes over. So the chain goes on by itself: Slurm on arc accepts a job submitted from inside a running job.

To stop the chain, cancel the waiting jobs first, then the running one:

squeue --me -n labdata-papers
scancel -u "$USER" -n labdata-papers -t PENDING
scancel <running job id>

If the chain breaks, submit scripts/papers/serve.sbatch again by hand. A new job does only what is due: a day with no daily pass, a month with no PMC sync after the 3rd, or a new build since the last PMC sync. The job log says successor not submitted when it could not submit a waiting job.

items.title: Watch it
items.text:
The job log, labdata-papers.<job id>.log, prints a line a minute. The first job writes it where sbatch --output says, or into the folder you submitted from. Each next job writes its log into the same folder. Between passes it looks like this:

2026-11-05T07:01Z idle; last daily pass 2026-11-05, last PMC sync 2026-11-03, copy pending: no

Each step can also run alone: labdata papers daily, labdata papers pmc-sync and labdata papers copy. Every pass ends with the copy, whatever it changed and whether it worked, run by hand or by the job. While a copy is pending, the job tries it again once an hour between passes, and a step run by hand exits 1.

items.title: Read paper-status.json
items.text:
The file at the paper store root says what the job did last and where the papers stand:

{
  "last_pass": {"kind": "daily", "start": "2026-11-05T00:30:02+00:00",
                "end": "2026-11-05T01:12:40+00:00", "outcome": "success"},
  "last_daily_success": "2026-11-05",
  "last_pmc_sync_success": "2026-11-03",
  "last_pmc_sync_build": "20261031T020000Z",
  "fetches": {"date": "2026-11-05", "by_tier": {"openalex": 300, "host": 2}},
  "quota": {"date": "2026-11-05", "by_key": {"a@lab.org": 100, "b@lab.org": 100, "c@lab.org": 100}},
  "counts": {"fetched": {"": 80512}, "waiting": {"openalex-backlog": 7690, "pmc-embargo": 1204},
             "manual": {"no-route": 9300, "host-blocked": 120}, "skipped": {"retracted": 41}},
  "copy_pending": false,
  "last_copy_success": "2026-11-05T01:12:41Z",
  "paperpile_pending": false
}
  • last_daily_success older than today, after 00:30 UTC, means a missed day.
  • last_pmc_sync_success is the date of the last PMC sync over all papers. A sampled sync leaves it alone.
  • last_pmc_sync_build is the GEO/SRA build that sync read. When the store's current build differs, the next PMC sync is due. A sampled sync leaves it alone too.
  • quota shows the copies each OpenAlex account bought today.
  • counts gives the papers per status, then per reason.
  • copy_pending: true means GCS is behind: the GCS login had expired, a copy failed or refused, or no full copy has worked yet. Log in, then run labdata papers copy, or labdata papers copy --full if the log asks for it. A copy that works sets it back to false.
  • last_copy_success is when the last copy that worked started. The next copy sends what changed after it.
  • finalized: true means GCS holds the store's last change: a copy sent this record.

The copy reads the changes from the files table, so it lists only the top level of the paper store and GCS. It sends paper-status.json last, after its copy record, marked finalized. It leaves out the lock file and the files a pass writes while it runs.

GCS keeps the paper store for good; the work disk is where passes run. So a copy deletes in GCS only the files that left the files table. It refuses, sending nothing, when the table is missing or empty, or when more than a small share of the copied files left it at once: the table may be damaged. The log says why, with the numbers. Check the table. If the files left on purpose, as when a change moves many files at once, run the copy by hand with the number of files the log gives. For 1200 files:

labdata papers copy --accept-deletes 1200

It sends the changes and deletes those files in GCS, up to that number.

items.title: When a pass refuses because the disk is behind
items.text: Each pass and each copy first checks that the work disk's copy record is the one in GCS. It compares the MD5 hash GCS keeps for that file with the disk's, and downloads nothing. If the two differ, the disk is behind GCS, or another disk has sent to GCS since. A disk with no copy record while GCS holds one was never restored, and refuses the same way. The pass then does nothing, marks the copy pending, and the log names the command that fixes it, labdata papers restore. Stop the paper job, restore as Restore the store from GCS shows, then start the job again. An expired login skips this check with a warning in the log.

items.title: Check the copy
items.text:
The routine check reads the status record and the copy record, and lists no paper folder. Run it between passes. The copy is current when both of these hold:

  • In paper-status.json, copy_pending is false and finalized is true: GCS holds the last change. If copy_pending is true, log in and run labdata papers copy.
  • The copy record in GCS matches the one on the disk. Each copy sends it last, after the files it lists:
pixi run rclone check "$LABDATA_PAPERS" <copy_to> --max-depth 1 \
  --include "/.copied-files.parquet"

It should report 0 differences and 1 matching file. It lists only the top level of each side.

A full check finds what differs when the copy record does not match, or after a change made in GCS by hand. It lists every file on both sides, so run it only to repair the copy, and only when the maintainer says yes. Run it between passes too: a pass that runs beside it changes files under it. Like the copy, it leaves out the hidden files. The status record differs once a pass has run since the last copy:

pixi run rclone check "$LABDATA_PAPERS" <copy_to> --one-way \
  --filter "- .*" --filter "- .*/**" --filter "- /paper-status.json"

It should report 0 differences. If it finds differences, labdata papers copy --full repairs them. It deletes nothing.

items.title: Restore the store from GCS
items.text:
Restore the work disk when it is new or lost, or when a pass refuses because the disk is behind GCS. Restore before the paper job runs again. An empty disk gets the whole store; a disk that fell behind gets only the files that changed. Downloads out of GCS cost money, so run a large restore only with the maintainer's yes.

Stop the paper job first, as Start the paper job shows. Then run the restore as its own job:

export LABDATA_PAPERS=/path/to/paper-store
sbatch --job-name=labdata-papers-restore --partition=cpu_batch \
  --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=8G --time=1-00:00:00 \
  --output=labdata-papers-restore.%j.log \
  --wrap "pixi run labdata papers restore --from <copy_to> --accept-download"

The restore prints how much it downloads. In a terminal it asks before more than 1 GB. A batch job has no terminal, so it needs --accept-download for that. Without the flag, a batch job prints the size and stops before a download of more than 1 GB.

If it stops, submit it again: it skips the files it already has. Then start the paper job. It finds the GEO/SRA store through LABDATA_STORE or the pointer, so a new cluster needs only that set.

The restore saves the copy record last, so the job's copies send only what changes from then on. It saves paper-status.json as the last copy left it, so the job knows when the last daily pass and the last PMC sync ran. It deletes the store's files that GCS does not hold, but leaves the hidden files of the disk alone, the daily pass's journal among them.

Restore before any copy by hand. A copy refuses, and sends nothing, on a disk with no copy record while GCS holds one. A full copy, labdata papers copy --full, also reads the list of files GCS holds, and refuses when the disk lacks more than a few of them. Its tables would replace the ones in GCS.

items.title: Copy the store to GCS
items.text: Google Cloud Storage (GCS) holds the store. A refresh or a build runs on a work disk on the cluster, and a copy then sends the new state to GCS. An update is done, or finalized, only once GCS holds it. If the work disk is lost or falls behind, a restore fills it from GCS. The tool that moves files is rclone, which comes with the pixi environment.

items.title: Set up once
items.text:
Make an rclone remote of type Google Cloud Storage, here called gcs:

pixi run rclone config

Then name the store's place in GCS in its labdata-store.toml:

copy_to = "gcs:<gcs-bucket>/<store>"

items.title: Log in each day
items.text:
Your Google login for rclone lasts one day. Renew it before a copy:

pixi run rclone config reconnect gcs:

A cluster node has no web browser. Answer n when rclone asks to use one. It then prints an rclone authorize ... command. Run that command on a computer with a browser, log in, and paste the token it prints back into the prompt on the node.

items.title: Prune and copy
items.text:
labdata store prune
labdata store copy

prune deletes builds and snapshots the current build no longer reads. It keeps each one for a grace period after it goes out of use, so a reader can finish; the API reference gives its length. --grace 0 deletes them at once: use it only as a one-off to tidy a store nobody is reading.

copy sends what changed since the last copy. GCS keeps the store for good, and the work disk is only where updates run, so a copy never deletes a file because the disk lacks it.

  • It sends the current build, the raw files and snapshots that build read, and the store's README.md. The marker file goes after them.
  • It then deletes in GCS, by name, the files the last copy sent that the current build no longer reads: the old build, a snapshot only that build read, a raw file the pack step dropped.
  • It sends refresh-status.json last, after its copy record, marked finalized. While an update has not switched to its new build, the copy leaves its status record on the disk, so GCS keeps the one before.
  • It leaves out work/ and support/. It will not run unless the current build is complete.

To know what changed, the copy keeps a hidden list of the files GCS holds, its copy record .copied-files.json, on the work disk and in GCS. When neither has the list, the copy makes it from the build that the marker file in GCS names. It does so only if that build is still on the disk, the last copy had worked, and a listing finds that build's files in GCS with the disk's sizes; it downloads nothing for that check. Otherwise, as for a store's first copy, labdata store copy stops and asks you to run this once:

labdata store copy --full

It sends the whole current state and deletes nothing. It lists every file on both sides, so keep it for a first copy or a repair. Later copies send only the changes.

A copy may always delete one raw file. It refuses, sending nothing, when it would delete more than that and more than a small share of the raw files: the build's manifest may be damaged. The message says why, with the numbers. If the files left on purpose, run the copy again with the count the message gives:

labdata store copy --accept-deletes <count>

A copy first checks the login with one listing call. When the login has expired, it stops, sends nothing and exits with an error:

rclone's Google login has expired, so GCS is behind the store. Run `rclone config reconnect gcs:`, then `labdata store copy`.

Log in, then run labdata store copy again. Files already sent are skipped. A refresh that meets an expired login ends built, not finalized: the work disk uses the new build, and refresh-status.json marks the copy pending until a copy works.

items.title: When the copy refuses because the disk is behind
items.text:
After the login check, a copy checks that the work disk's copy record is the one in GCS. It compares the MD5 hash GCS keeps for that file with the disk's, and downloads nothing. Every update makes the same check when it starts: a refresh, a full run, a build by hand and the SRA removal. If the two differ, the disk is behind GCS, or another disk has sent to GCS since. A disk with no copy record while GCS holds one was never restored, and refuses the same way. The copy then sends nothing, marks the copy pending, and names the command that fixes it:

the work disk's copy record, .copied-files.json, is not the one in GCS at gcs:<gcs-bucket>/<store>, so nothing was sent: this disk is behind GCS, or another disk sent to it since. Run `labdata store restore --from gcs:<gcs-bucket>/<store>` to bring the work disk in step with GCS.

Run the restore, then the copy or the update again. When GCS holds no copy record at all, but the disk does, GCS is new or was emptied: the copy asks for labdata store copy --full.

items.title: Check the copy
items.text:
The routine check reads the status record and the copy record, and lists no store folder. The last update is finalized when both of these hold:

  • In refresh-status.json, outcome is finalized and copy_pending is false. If copy_pending is true, log in and run labdata store copy.
  • The copy record in GCS matches the one on the disk. Each copy sends it last, after the files it lists:
pixi run rclone check "$LABDATA_STORE" <copy_to> --max-depth 1 \
  --include "/.copied-files.json"

It should report 0 differences and 1 matching file. It lists only the top level of each side.

A full check finds what differs when the copy record does not match, or after a change made in GCS by hand. It reads every file on both sides, so run it only to repair the copy, and only when the maintainer says yes. It leaves out what the copy leaves out:

pixi run rclone check "$LABDATA_STORE" <copy_to> \
  --filter "- .*" --filter "- .*/**" --filter "- /work/**" \
  --filter "- /support/**" \
  --filter "- /builds/<old build>/**"

It should report 0 differences. A build or snapshot that prune keeps for its grace period is not in GCS: add a filter for each one instead of counting it as a difference. A file found only in GCS is one a copy should have deleted. If it finds files missing from GCS, labdata store copy --full sends them. It deletes nothing.

items.title: Restore the store from GCS
items.text:
Restore the work disk when it is new or lost, or when a copy or an update refuses because the disk is behind GCS. Restore before the next update:

labdata store restore --root /path/to/store --from gcs:<gcs-bucket>/<store>

On a disk that already has the store's marker, --from defaults to its copy_to.

  • It reads the copy record in GCS and downloads what the disk lacks or holds differently. An empty disk gets the whole current state; a disk that fell behind gets only the difference. A file already on the disk with the size and hash GCS gives is not downloaded again.
  • It deletes the files the disk's copy record names and the one in GCS does not, such as an old build. On a disk with no copy record, it deletes every file in builds/, raw/ and snapshots/ that GCS's copy record does not name.
  • It leaves work/, support/ and extracts/ alone. A build makes a missing extract from its snapshot.
  • It saves the copy record and refresh-status.json last, as GCS holds them. The status record then says finalized, so the next refresh knows when the last one ran.
  • It holds the store's run lock, so it refuses while an update runs. If it says it cannot check that update and you know it has ended, add --owner-gone.

It prints how much it downloads, and asks before more than 1 GB. Downloads out of GCS cost money, so a large restore needs the maintainer's yes. A batch job has no terminal to ask in: pass --accept-download to let it download more than 1 GB. If it stops, run it again: it skips the files it already has.

items.title: Read the store on another computer
items.text:
To only read the store, copy just the marker and the build it names, and point labdata at it:

rclone copy gcs:<gcs-bucket>/<store> /data/store \
  --include "/labdata-store.toml" --include "/builds/<build>/**"

items.title: How the stores work
items.text:
Two stores live on a work disk on the cluster. The GEO/SRA store keeps study metadata from NCBI. The paper store keeps the papers those studies link to. Google Cloud Storage (GCS) holds both and is the source of truth. An update is done only once GCS holds it.

This page shows how data moves from its sources to GCS. Each colour in its diagrams means one thing: the GEO/SRA store, the paper store, GCS, a failure and an update or paper set aside. To run a store, follow Run the full download, Copy the store to GCS or Run the paper store.

items.title: From the sources to GCS
items.text:
The GEO/SRA store takes its records from NCBI. The paper store reads which papers to fetch from the current GEO/SRA build, then fetches each paper from the cheapest source that has it. Both stores copy their changes to GCS, and a new work disk restores from GCS.

NCBI sources feed the GEO/SRA store; PMC, PubMed, OpenAlex and publisher sites feed the paper store, which reads its paper links from the current build. Each store copies to its own GCS path and restores from it. SOURCES WORK DISK ON THE CLUSTER GCS For the GEO/SRA store NCBI FTP bulk files SRA, BioProject, BioSample E-utilities esummary a summary of every Series GEO download site family SOFT, file list E-utilities efetch SRA experiment XML For the paper store PMC Open Access bucket XML, figures, supplements PubMed and the PMC ID converter details, IDs, retractions OpenAlex paid PDFs Publisher sites free PDF links Paperpile papers saved by hand GEO/SRA store labdata-store.toml the marker: names the current build snapshots/ bulk files, summaries extract extracts/ Parquet tables raw/ fetched records build builds/<id>/ one per update, never changed once written monthly refresh per Series PMID and DOI links Paper store Four tables papers, paper_info, files, attempts papers/ one folder per paper, by PMID or DOI paper-status.json the status of each pass manual-queue.nbib the manual queue PMC sync daily pass the queue gcs:<gcs-bucket>/ <store> the current build and the files it reads refresh-status.json sent last copy restore gcs:<gcs-bucket>/ datalake/paper-store the tables and paper folders paper-status.json sent last copy restore Records flow from their sources through the work disk to GCS.

Each source gives the stores these records:

  • NCBI FTP bulk files: the lists of SRA, BioProject and BioSample records, each month.
  • E-utilities esummary: a summary of every GEO Series, each month.
  • The GEO download site: each Series' family SOFT file and its supplementary file list.
  • E-utilities efetch: the SRA experiment XML for each Series.
  • The PMC Open Access bucket: article XML, figures and supplements.
  • PubMed and the PMC ID converter: each paper's details, IDs and retraction notices.
  • OpenAlex: work details, and PDFs bought within a daily quota.
  • Publisher sites: free PDF links.

items.title: The GEO/SRA store keeps one build per update
items.text:
For each target GEO Series, the store holds the Series with its Samples and Platforms. It also holds the linked SRA studies, experiments, runs and samples, and the BioProject and BioSample records. Each update makes a new build, a complete set of tables that never changes once written. A small marker file names the current build, and readers open that one through BuildReader.

A full run and a monthly refresh are Snakemake workflows. Each step runs once its inputs exist. Only a few network steps run at once, so the store stays gentle on NCBI.

The update workflow. A refresh downloads snapshots and patches the GEO Series list; both runs pick the target Series, fetch them in the GEO and SRA lanes and pack the parts into raw/. A refresh also lists the changes and confirms withdrawn Series. Every update ends with extract, build, switch, prune and copy to GCS. WHAT TO FETCH FETCH AND PACK BUILD AND COPY Snapshots FTP bulk files GEO Series list patch the summaries snapshots Targets the Series to hold targets Changes what to fetch again Series to fetch GEO lane SOFT and file lists SRA lane, pass 1 beside the GEO lane SOFT files SRA lane, pass 2 experiments the SOFT adds fetch results Confirm withdrawn Series parts Pack parts into raw/ raw/ snapshots Extract snapshots to Parquet Parquet Build a new build new build Switch check coverage, move the marker marker Prune builds out of use changes Copy to GCS Every update ends the same way: extract, build, switch, prune and copy.

The dashed steps run only in a refresh. A refresh downloads new snapshots and fetches again only the GEO Series that changed. Before it packs, it confirms which Series NCBI withdrew. A Series goes only when a fetch of that Series alone finds it gone. A full run skips the dashed steps and fetches every target Series from the snapshots on disk. The SRA lane runs twice because each saved SOFT file can name more SRA experiments.

items.title: Each update ends finalized, failed or abandoned
items.text:
The status record, refresh-status.json, names the outcome of the last update.

The states of one update: running, then built after the switch, then finalized once the copy sends the status record last. A running update that fails can resume, or is abandoned when a new update replaces it. take the run lock running holds the run lock coverage passes, switch built the work disk reads the new build resume copy, status record last finalized GCS holds the build and the status record copy failed: the next run copies first a step fails, or the new build misses too many target Series failed readers keep the old build a new update replaces it, or a refresh waits too long abandoned only the run folder records it An update is finalized only once GCS holds its status record.
  • running: the update holds the run lock. It starts only when the work disk matches GCS.
  • failed: a step failed, or the new build missed too many target Series. Readers keep the old build. The next run resumes in the same folder.
  • abandoned: a new update replaced it. A refresh that waits too long to resume is abandoned too. Only the run folder records this outcome.
  • built: the work disk reads the new build, but GCS does not hold it yet. If the copy fails, the next run copies first.
  • finalized: GCS holds the new build and the status record.

When the run lock is held, the store asks Slurm whether the job that took it still runs. If it has ended, the next update takes the lock. If Slurm cannot tell, you confirm with --owner-gone.

items.title: The paper store climbs a ladder of sources
items.text:
The paper store fetches the papers that target GEO Series and held BioProjects link by PMID or DOI. It reads those links from the current GEO/SRA build, so a new build brings in new papers. Each paper waits on the first tier that can still serve it, cheapest first:

The tier ladder: an older paper tries the PMC bucket, then an OpenAlex PDF, then a publisher link, then the manual queue in Paperpile. The tier that serves it marks it fetched. A recent paper waits for PMC and tries only the free tiers. A retracted paper is skipped. Waits for PMC published within the last 365 days recent free tiers only New paper a PMID or DOI the build links older TIER 1 PMC bucket free, monthly no copy or failed TIER 2 OpenAlex PDF paid quota, daily no copy or failed TIER 3 Publisher link free, daily blocked or failed Manual queue saved by hand in Paperpile XML or PDF PDF PDF a later PMC sync fetched PMC's files later replace any other PDF skipped a retracted paper, whatever its state Each paper climbs from the cheapest tier until one serves it.
  • A tier that has no copy, or fails, passes the paper on. Repeated server errors pass it on too.
  • A paper published within the last 365 days waits for PMC and tries only the free tiers.
  • A retracted paper is skipped, whatever its state.
  • PMC gives the article XML, figures and supplements, where the other tiers give only a PDF. When PMC later has a paper, the PMC sync saves its files and then deletes the other PDF.

One long Slurm job, the paper job, runs two kinds of pass:

  • The daily pass, after 00:30 UTC: buy PDFs from OpenAlex within each account's daily quota, try each publisher link once, then rewrite the manual queue.
  • The PMC sync, on the 3rd of each month and whenever a new GEO/SRA build becomes current: take in new papers, look up their details, then fetch what changed in the PMC bucket.

Every pass takes the store's lock, checks that the work disk matches GCS, does its work and saves all four tables together. It ends with a copy to GCS. The paper job keeps two more jobs queued behind it, so a new one takes over when its time on Slurm runs out.

items.title: Both stores copy to GCS the same way
items.text:
A copy starts with a check. It compares the copy record that GCS holds with the one on the work disk. If they differ, the work disk is behind GCS, so the copy refuses and you restore first. Then the copy sends, in this order:

  1. The new or changed files, by name.
  2. The top-level files, such as the marker and README.md.
  3. The deletes, by name.
  4. The copy record: the list of files GCS now holds.
  5. The status record, marked finalized.

Because the status record goes last, GCS never holds a status record for files it lacks. No copy mirrors the disk with rclone sync. A guard stops a copy that would delete more raw files or paper files than a small share of them, unless you allow it. A restore runs the same steps the other way, and asks before a large download.

items.title: When each store changes
items.text:
When GEO/SRA store Paper store Each day Nothing runs. The daily pass, then a copy. Each hour, if needed Nothing runs. A failed pass or a pending copy runs again. Each month The refresh, started by hand in the maintenance run. The PMC sync on the 3rd, or as soon as a new build is current. Each year Heavy checks, the refresh, then removal of withdrawn SRA records, a new build and a copy. Nothing extra runs. After a store code change One full build at the end. Nothing extra runs.

The maintenance log records each monthly and yearly run.

items.title: Run the full download
items.text:
One command fetches every target GEO Series and the records it links to, builds the tables and copies the store to GCS. It runs on the cluster as one Slurm job, and you can stop and restart it at any time.

GCS holds the store, and updates run on a work disk on the cluster. Every update, the full download and the monthly refresh alike, goes through the same steps:

  1. Restore, by hand and only when the work disk is empty or behind GCS. See Restore the store from GCS.
  2. Update: fetch, pack and build.
  3. Check the new build's coverage.
  4. Switch the work disk to the new build. Readers on the cluster use it from now on. Then prune deletes the builds out of use.
  5. Finalize: copy the store to GCS. The update is done only once GCS holds it.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Download the bulk snapshots with scripts/bulk/download_ncbi_bulk.py. The run uses the newest snapshot of each source.
  • Save your NCBI email and API key with labdata ncbi configure.
  • To copy the store at the end, set copy_to in labdata-store.toml and log in to rclone that day. See Copy the store to GCS. Without copy_to, the run skips the copy and says so.
  • Every update first checks the work disk against GCS: a run, a refresh, a build by hand and the SRA removal. If the disk is behind, or has no copy record while GCS holds one, the update stops and names the labdata store restore command to run.

items.title: Start a round
items.text:
Run the download in three rounds: 1%, then 10%, then all of the target list. Each round's Series are a fixed random sample, and a smaller round's Series are all inside the next one. A larger round never fetches again what a smaller round saved.

From the repository folder on the cluster:

export LABDATA_STORE=/path/to/store
sbatch scripts/store/run.sbatch 0.01   # round 1
sbatch scripts/store/run.sbatch 0.1    # round 2
sbatch scripts/store/run.sbatch        # round 3: every target Series

Start the next round only when the last one looks right. Off a cluster, or for a quick try, run the same steps straight away:

labdata store run --fraction 0.01

In a held Slurm job reached over ssh, labdata sees the whole node: first set the job's cores and memory in MB, such as export SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE=24 SLURM_MEM_PER_NODE=98304.

items.title: Watch it
items.text:
The job log, labdata-run.<job id>.log, shows each step as it starts and ends. The fetch steps print a line at least once a minute:

2026-10-15 21:04:10 labdata.store.geo_lane 1,204/1,985 Series SOFT, round 1 (60.7%), 26.8/s, errors: timeout 3, finish ~2026-10-15 21:05 UTC

Each step also writes its own log under work/run/<snapshot date>-<fraction>/logs/ in the store. That folder holds the round's markers too: one file per finished step.

At the end, the coverage step checks that every Series in the round is held or explained:

Target Series: 1985 (geo-series snapshot 2026-10-14)
Held: 1983
Gaps: 2
  soft-missing: 2
  fetch-failed: 0
  withdrawn: 0
  unexplained: 0
SRA experiments fetch-failed: 0 (not Series gaps)
Coverage passes.

If coverage fails, the run stops there. The store keeps its old build, and the run deletes nothing and copies nothing.

items.title: Resume
items.text:
Submit the same command again. The run starts at the first step that did not finish, and the fetch steps skip every Series and experiment already saved. A job that the cluster stops to make room is put back in the queue and resumes by itself.

The fetch steps ask once more for every item that failed before they finish. A Series that still fails is a fetch-failed gap, and an SRA experiment that still fails is counted on the SRA experiments fetch-failed line. To ask for those again, submit the same round again: the fetch steps ask only for what failed, and the steps after them run again. Nothing saved is fetched twice.

items.title: After the last round
items.text:
To keep each round's logs with the store, copy them into support/. <round> is the round's folder under work/run/, such as 2026-10-14-all:

scripts/store/keep_run_logs.sh "$LABDATA_STORE" <round>

The build writes README.md at the store root. It says what each folder holds, how it was made, and how to open the store as a database. After you copy logs into support/ or clean work/, write it again with fresh folder sizes:

labdata store readme

The run keeps the old build for a grace period after the switch, so a reader that opened it can finish; the API reference gives its length. labdata store prune --grace 0 deletes it and the snapshots only it read at once. Use that only as a one-off to tidy a store nobody is reading, not as a refresh step. Prune never deletes the current build or anything it reads.

items.title: Refresh the store
items.text:
Once the full download is done, one command a month keeps the store current. It downloads new snapshots, fetches the GEO Series that changed or appeared since the last successful refresh, removes the GEO Series that a fetch confirms are withdrawn, builds, checks coverage, switches, prunes and copies. Run it from the repository folder:

labdata store refresh

On a Slurm cluster, run it as one job:

export LABDATA_STORE=/path/to/store
sbatch scripts/store/refresh.sbatch

The first refresh searches for changes from the date of the geo-series snapshot the current build read; each later one, from the last successful refresh, less a few days of overlap (labdata store refresh --help gives the number). To search from another date, add --since YYYY-MM-DD.

If it stops, run the same command again. It goes on in the same folder, work/refresh/<start time>/, from the first unfinished step, and asks for nothing it saved. That folder holds the refresh's markers and logs.

A refresh removes a GEO Series only when GEO no longer lists it, or the refresh got no record for it, and a fetch of it alone then says it is gone. It keeps every SRA record.

A refresh that stopped before its switch is not resumed if it started more than 7 days ago, or an older version of liulab-data started it. The next run starts a new one from the same date, and labdata store prune deletes the old folder. A refresh that switched and only failed to copy is finished by the next run's copy, however old it is.

A refresh, a full run, a build, the SRA removal and a prune each refuse to start while another of them runs on the store. So do a fetch, pack, extract or copy that you run by hand. If the message says it cannot check whether the other one still runs, check with squeue on its cluster. Once you know it has ended, run the same command again with --owner-gone.

A refresh killed inside a job that still runs, such as a held interactive job, looks alive from another node, because Slurm says its job runs. Start the next refresh on the same node: there the check asks the process itself.

refresh-status.json in the store root shows the outcome:

{
  "update": "refresh",
  "build": "20261107T020000Z",
  "started": "2026-11-07T02:00:00Z",
  "ended": "2026-11-07T03:24:10Z",
  "outcome": "finalized",
  "since": "2026-10-14",
  "last_success": "2026-11-07",
  "folder": "work/refresh/2026-11-07T020000Z",
  "counts": {"geo-soft": {"added": 2410, "replaced": 4180, "removed": 12}},
  "copy_pending": false,
  "copy_pending_at_switch": false
}

The outcome is one of these:

Outcome Meaning running The refresh runs, or was killed before it could say so. failed It stopped before the switch. The store keeps its old build. built The work disk uses the new build, but GCS does not hold it yet. finalized GCS holds the new build. The refresh is done.

last_success changes only once the store has switched to the new build. When rclone's login has expired, the refresh ends built, copy_pending is true, and the job exits with an error. Log in, then run the same refresh command again: it does only the copy. labdata store copy does the same. If the copy asks for --full, run labdata store copy --full. copy_pending_at_switch keeps copy_pending as it was when the refresh switched builds.

To keep the refresh's step logs with the store, copy them into support/. <started> is the refresh's folder under work/refresh/, which refresh-status.json names:

scripts/store/keep_run_logs.sh "$LABDATA_STORE" refresh/<started>

Then, once refresh-status.json says finalized and while no update runs, you may delete everything in work/. The Parquet extracts of the snapshots sit in extracts/, outside work/. A build that needs a missing one makes it again, slowly. The store's README.md lists what is safe to delete.

items.title: What a refresh needs
items.text:
Every step can be killed and run again. The figures below come from the first full-store refresh, a month after the last fetch, with 32 CPUs and 90 GB. A dash means no load worth counting; "not measured" means the step did not run in that refresh.

Step CPU Memory Scratch disk Network (NCBI, GEO, GCS) Wall time snapshots 1 core 1 GB 43 GB new 45 GB from NCBI FTP 5 min geo-series 1 core not measured 0.2 GB new 33 E-utilities calls 1 min, measured alone targets 1 core 1 GB – – 1 min changes 1 core 1 GB – 1 E-utilities search 2 min geo 1 core 4 GB 2 GB 6,500 GEO FTP requests, 1.6 GB 9 min eutils (beside and after the GEO lane) 1 core 4 GB 1 GB 320 E-utilities calls, 0.7 GB 12 min, then 4 min extract (each source) up to 37 cores up to 38 GB 18 GB – 10 min (biosample), under 1 min (others) confirm 1 core 1 GB – one E-utilities call per removal candidate not measured pack 1 core 3 GB rewrites the raw buckets it touches – 7 min build not measured not measured 22 GB, one build – 44 min in the last full build switch, after the coverage check not measured prune not measured copy not measured the store, to GCS

items.title: Yearly
items.text:
Once a year, add five heavy steps to that month's refresh. Each one either takes hours or loads NCBI more than a refresh does, so none of them runs in a normal month. Run them in this order. The first two check the current build, so run them before the refresh:

  1. Open every record. Check the current build with the network blocked:

    pixi run python scripts/store/check_stage1.py --every-record

    Without --every-record, the script runs only the thin-slice checks of a few chosen records, as after a normal refresh. The flag adds two passes over every record held: each one opens, and its hash matches its raw text.

  2. Rebuild with no network and compare. Make a scratch store from the store's raw files and snapshots, build it, and compare it with the current build. Hard links cost no extra disk, and the store itself is only read:

    scratch=/path/to/scratch
mkdir "$scratch"
grep -v '^copy_to' "$LABDATA_STORE/labdata-store.toml" > "$scratch/labdata-store.toml"
cp -al "$LABDATA_STORE/raw" "$LABDATA_STORE/snapshots" "$scratch/"
unshare -rn labdata store build --root "$scratch" --build-id offline
pixi run python scripts/store/compare_builds.py \
  "$LABDATA_STORE/builds/<current build>" "$scratch/builds/offline"

    The scratch marker leaves out copy_to, so the build checks nothing against GCS. The build first makes the extracts of the snapshots it reads, in the scratch store. unshare -rn blocks the network; leave it out where the node does not allow it. The compare prints each difference and ends with the builds match when there is none. Delete the scratch store after.

  3. Fetch the whole Series list again. A monthly refresh patches the geo-series snapshot: it fetches only the Series GEO marks as new or changed. GEO sometimes changes a Series without moving its update date, so once a year fetch every summary. Do it on the day of the refresh, before it starts, so the refresh uses this snapshot:

    python -I scripts/bulk/download_ncbi_bulk.py "$LABDATA_STORE/snapshots" \
  --date YYYY-MM-DD --full geo-series

    Then run the refresh as usual.

  4. Remove withdrawn SRA records. After the refresh, remove the SRA experiments and runs that NCBI no longer serves. Each one goes only after a fetch of it alone confirms it gone. Then pack and build to apply the removals, and copy the store to finalize them:

    labdata store remove-sra --root "$LABDATA_STORE"
labdata store pack
labdata store build
labdata store copy

    If it stops, run it again: it goes on where it stopped and asks again for any that failed. The removal is done once refresh-status.json says finalized. The decision record says why this runs once a year.

  5. Time the queries on a quiet node. Run the full benchmark on the new build, on the least loaded node. Other jobs on the node slow the reads, so keep the node's load with the timings. The partition may not give a whole node, so ask for 16 CPUs and 64 GB on it:

    sinfo -N -o "%N %O" --sort=O
LABDATA_STORE=/path/to/store sbatch --nodelist=NODE --cpus-per-task=16 --mem=64G \
  --output=OUT/bench.%j.log scripts/store/benchmark.sbatch OUT

    sinfo lists each node with its load, lowest first; put the first one for NODE. The job prints the node's load average, then each query's wall time and memory against its limit.

items.title: What a yearly run adds
items.text:
Rough figures, measured on the full store in 2026. The rebuild and the removal each add a full build, about an hour. "Not measured" means no full-store run has timed it yet.

Step CPU Memory Network Wall time Open every record 1 core about 60 GB none about 3 h Rebuild and compare up to 32 cores about 60 GB, with DuckDB's share capped none about 1 h to build; the compare is not measured Whole Series list 1 core 1 GB about 600 E-utilities calls about 40 min SRA removal 1 core not measured one E-utilities call per batch of candidates not measured; inferred about 1 h, then an hour to pack and build Benchmark a whole node up to 128 GB none not measured; the job asks for up to 4 h

items.title: Make a sample build
items.text:
A sample build is a small copy of a full store's tables, for trying a change before you build the whole store. It holds a fixed random share of each record type, made by the same code that makes a full build. Give it the full store, an empty folder for the sample and the share:

labdata store build --sample-of /path/to/store --root /path/to/scratch --fraction 0.01

The full store is only read: its raw files, snapshots and current build stay as they are. The sample is built in the scratch folder, which becomes a store of its own, so open_store("/path/to/scratch") opens it. A scratch folder takes samples of one store only. The same share always picks the same records, and a smaller share's records are all inside a larger one's. Notes are the exception: they can differ between shares.

Series and SRA experiments hold about the share you asked for. Samples, platforms, BioProjects and BioSamples hold more, because they also hold what the sampled records link to.

To time queries on the sample:

pixi run python scripts/store/benchmark.py /path/to/scratch

The benchmark also prints the share of links whose far end the sample holds. Most links point outside a sample, so its link-query timings are indicative only.

items.title: Cut a store down to a list of Series
items.text:
A subset is a small store that holds only the Series you list and the records they link to. It has the tables and layout of a full store, so the same code reads it, and it is small enough for a laptop. Write the Series accessions one a line, then give the full store, the list and an empty folder:

labdata store subset --from /path/to/store --series series.txt --root /path/to/small

The full store is only read. The command prints how many records of each type it kept and the bytes it wrote:

Cut build 20261114T020000Z to /path/to/small/builds/20261114T020000Z-subset
BioProject: 3
GEO Platform: 2
GEO Sample: 2
GEO Series: 2
SRA experiment: 2
SRA run: 2
SRA sample: 2
SRA study: 2
not listed, so not held: GSE246308 SubSeries of GSE246310
Wrote 140009 bytes

The subset follows links forward only: from a Series to its Samples, their experiments and runs, and each record's Platform and BioProject. A paper or a BioProject that other Series share adds none of those Series. The last line but one names a Series outside your list that a listed Series belongs to; add it to the list if you want it. open_store("/path/to/small") opens the subset. Unlike a sample build, it copies rows and reads no raw file, so it has no raw/ or snapshots/ and cannot be refreshed: run the command again to change the list.

To take the papers of those Series too, cut the paper store with the subset you just made:

labdata papers subset --from /path/to/papers --store /path/to/small --root /path/to/small-papers

It copies the rows and the files of each paper that a Series or BioProject in the subset links, and prints the papers, the files and the bytes. The full paper store is only read. The command stops with a message if the paper job is saving its tables at that moment; run it again then. Neither small store names a bucket, so no copy command run on one can reach the full stores' copies. To read both:

export LABDATA_STORE=/path/to/small LABDATA_PAPERS=/path/to/small-papers

items.title: Go deeper
items.text: The steps are also commands of their own: labdata store pack, build, coverage, prune and copy. Run labdata store --help to list them, and see the API reference for the modules behind them.

items.title: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ
items.text: This tutorial goes from a GEO accession to downloaded FASTQ in a few short steps, using a real study — GSE47966 (Global epigenomic reconfiguration during mammalian brain development). First, make sure you've installed the package and set your NCBI email.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: 1. Look up a GEO Series
items.text:
Start from any GEO accession (GSE…). Building the handle is instant; reading a field is what triggers the lookup.

from labdata import Series

gse = Series("GSE47966")     # just a handle — no network yet

gse.title         # 'Global epigenomic reconfiguration during mammalian brain development'
gse.organism      # 'Homo sapiens; Mus musculus'
gse.platforms     # [Platform('GPL13112'), Platform('GPL11154')]
gse.samples       # [Sample('GSM1173819'), Sample('GSM1173773'), ...]   (65 samples)
gse.experiments   # [Experiment('SRX314994'), Experiment('SRX314993'), ...]   (65 experiments)
gse.url           # 'https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE47966'

Each linked item (a sample, an experiment, a run) is its own object you can drill into the same way. See the API reference for everything they expose.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: 2. Get the SRA run table
items.text:
Want the table you'd normally click through on NCBI's SRA Run Selector — one row per sequencing run, with library and instrument details? Ask for it directly. It comes back as a pandas DataFrame, so you can filter, sort, and export it however you like.

table = gse.make_sra_run_table()      # one row per run (392 in this study)

table[["Run", "Instrument", "ReadStructure", "Bases", "LibraryLayout"]].head(3)

         Run           Instrument ReadStructure        Bases LibraryLayout
0  SRR907554  Illumina HiSeq 2000            50  10100000000        SINGLE
1  SRR907555  Illumina HiSeq 2000            50  10100000000        SINGLE
2  SRR907556  Illumina HiSeq 2000            50  10100000000        SINGLE
...

ReadStructure gives the length of each read in a spot, joined with +: a single-end 50 bp run reads 50, while a paired run with a 28 bp barcode and a 94 bp cDNA read reads 28+94 — a quick way to spot single-cell chemistries.

table.to_csv("GSE47966_runs.csv", index=False)   # hand it off to collaborators
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: 3. Download all FASTQ files
items.text:
One call fetches the FASTQ for every run in the study, running a Snakemake pipeline (prefetch → extract → compress) over sra-tools under the hood. Files are organized by study → experiment → run and gzipped for you:

gse.download("./fastq", ncbi_parallel=3, cores=16)   # ≤3 downloads at once, 16 cores total

The two knobs are independent, which is the point: ncbi_parallel caps how many runs prefetch from NCBI at once (keep it low to stay friendly with NCBI), while cores bounds total CPU for the local extraction/gzip work. So downloads keep the network busy while cores chew through already-fetched runs, instead of the two blocking each other. On an HPC allocation, set cores to your allotted cores.

{'SRR921999': True, 'SRR922000': True, 'SRR922001': True, ...}     # each run: success?

The files land in a tidy tree:

fastq/
└── GSE47966/
    ├── SRX314994/
    │   ├── SRR921999.fastq.gz
    │   ├── SRR922000.fastq.gz
    │   └── ...
    └── SRX314993/
        └── ...

Good to know

  • This downloads real sequencing data, which can be large — point output_dir somewhere with room to spare. If free space looks tight, the download prints a rough warning before it starts (it never blocks).
  • GSE47966's runs are single-end, so each gives one .fastq.gz; paired-end runs produce _1/_2 files instead.
  • Interruptible. A finished run leaves a .<run>.done marker, so re-running download() skips what's already done — an interrupted download resumes without re-fetching SRA data (and prefetch itself resumes a partial .sra). Safe after a Ctrl-C or an HPC walltime kill.
  • Modest peak disk. Snakemake reclaims each intermediate the moment the next step consumes it — a run's .sra the moment its FASTQ is extracted, the uncompressed FASTQ the moment they're gzipped — and drains extraction/compression before fetching more, so only a handful of .sra sit on disk at once. Lower ncbi_parallel to shrink that working set further.
  • Pass keep_sra=True to keep each run's .sra next to its FASTQ instead of reclaiming it after extraction (useful for re-extracting later), or prefetch_only=True to just stage the .sra files without extracting.
  • Needs sra-tools and pigz on your system (see Installation); Snakemake comes with liulab-data.

Just one experiment?

Series.download does the whole study. To grab a single experiment instead, use SraDownloader — see the API reference. Pass original=True for that experiment's original-format files.

Have a BioProject instead?

BioProject exposes the same download() — BioProject("PRJNA1027859").download("./fastq") lays the FASTQ out identically, under a PRJNA…/ directory. The labdata geo download command auto-detects which you gave it, so GSE… and PRJ… accessions both just work.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: When the .sra is missing or useless
items.text:
Sometimes a run's SRA-normalized .sra is gone or wrong. For example, a 10X run's .sra may keep only one read of a pair. The submitter's original-format files (listed under "Data access" in the SRA Run Browser) are still there. Name those experiments with original_srx to fetch them as-is. This downloads only; it does not extract:

gse.download("./fastq", original_srx=["SRX34567890"])

labdata geo download GSE310667 --original-srx SRX34567890

The files land under …/<SRX>/<SRR>/ with their original names and are md5-checked against NCBI. Everything else in the study still takes the normal sra-tools path. This only sets the mode. To also narrow which experiments run, add --select-srx/select_srx (repeatable, or a whitelist file). Original format varies from study to study, so labdata downloads it and leaves the processing to you. It needs curl in addition to sra-tools/pigz. When the original file is a 10x cellranger BAM, the 10x BAM → FASTQ tutorial turns it back into remap-ready FASTQ.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: 4. Grab the supplementary files
items.text:
Raw FASTQ isn't the whole story. Authors usually attach supplementary files — processed matrices, peak calls, bigWigs, READMEs — to the Series. List them and grab their download URLs directly:

gse.supplementary_files       # ['GSE47966_RAW.tar', 'GSE47966_README.txt', 'filelist.txt']
gse.supplementary_file_urls   # full https URLs you can download
gse.supplementary_http_url    # the suppl/ directory itself

These are often where the useful, ready-to-analyze outputs live — see what's not in GEO for why they matter.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: Going deeper
items.text: This tutorial covers the common path. For the full picture — every property of Series, Sample, Platform, Experiment, Run, and BioProject, plus the downloader options — head to the API reference.
path: GEO Series: from study to FASTQ

items.title: Recovering FASTQ from a 10x cellranger BAM
items.text:
Some 10x Genomics studies upload a cellranger BAM as their raw data, and SRA's normalized .sra for those runs is unusable — often it kept only one read of the pair, so fasterq-dump can't reconstruct the barcodes. The fix is to go back to the submitter's original BAM and turn that into FASTQ with 10x's own bamtofastq, which reads the 10x tags to split the barcode (R1), cDNA (R2), and index (I1) reads correctly — ready to remap with STARsolo.

This is a two-step flow: download the original BAMs, then convert them.
path: Recovering FASTQ from a 10x cellranger BAM

items.title: 1. Download the original-format BAMs
items.text:
Fetch the submitter's files for the affected experiments (see the GEO Series tutorial's note on original files):

labdata geo download GSE208154 --original-srx SRX16000000 -o ./data

They land under ./data/GSE208154/<SRX>/<SRR>/<name>.bam.
path: Recovering FASTQ from a 10x cellranger BAM

items.title: 2. Convert the BAMs to FASTQ
items.text:
labdata tenx bamtofastq GSE208154 -o ./data --cores 16

labdata tenx bamtofastq auto-detects which runs carry a 10x BAM (from the SRA Data Locator listing) and converts each one that's on disk, driving bamtofastq as a Snakemake DAG. The result is laid out like the download pipeline — flat under the experiment directory, one prefix per run — so a later STARsolo step parses one layout:

data/GSE208154/<SRX>/
  <SRR>_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz   # barcode + UMI
  <SRR>_S1_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz   # cDNA
  <SRR>_S1_L001_I1_001.fastq.gz   # sample index
  …

The R1/R2/I1 and lane markers are preserved (STARsolo needs them), while the files sit flat beside the experiment's other runs and glob as <SRX>/<SRR>*.fastq.gz, just like a normal download.

Good to know

  • Conversion-only. This step reads BAMs that are already on disk; run the original-format download first. Pointing both commands at the same -o directory is intended — they share the <GSE>/<SRX>/<SRR>/ layout.
  • Interruptible. A finished run leaves a .<run>.tenx.done marker, so re-running skips what's already converted. Safe after a Ctrl-C or HPC walltime kill.
  • --cores bounds total CPU across runs; --threads-per-run sets each bamtofastq's --nthreads. On an HPC allocation, pass --cores $SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE.
  • Auto-detection uses one SDL lookup per run. Pass --all-runs to skip it and convert every run of the selected experiments (e.g. when you already know they're all 10x), or --select-srx to narrow which experiments are considered.
  • On an offline HPC compute node, pass --from-disk: the run list is built by scanning the downloaded <SRX>/<SRR>/*.bam tree instead of querying NCBI, so no network or credentials are needed.
  • Pass --remove-bam to delete each run's source BAM once its FASTQ are produced — it reclaims the large original, and only fires after a run converts successfully (an interrupted run keeps its BAM for the resumed rerun).
  • Needs 10x_bamtofastq on your system (see Installation); Snakemake comes with liulab-data.

From Python, TenxConverter is the equivalent entry point:

from labdata import TenxConverter

TenxConverter("GSE208154", "./data").convert(cores=16)

See the API reference for the full signature.

items.title: Understanding GEO & SRA
items.text: New to NCBI's sequencing databases? This page gives you just enough of the mental model to use labdata confidently. For the hands-on walkthrough, see the GEO Series tutorial.

items.title: Two databases, one study
items.text:
A sequencing study usually lives in two linked NCBI databases:

  • GEO — the processed, expression-focused side (count matrices, the study's description, sample list).
  • SRA — the raw reads side (the actual FASTQ files you download).

GEO records point into SRA, so you can start from a GEO accession and follow the links all the way down to raw data.

items.title: The hierarchy: study → sample → experiment → run
items.text:
Everything is organized as a tree, from a big project down to individual FASTQ files. Each level has its own ID prefix — and its own class in labdata:

Level Example ID What it is labdata class BioProject PRJNA208503 the whole study / "the paper" BioProject GEO Series GSE47966 the study, as seen in GEO Series GEO Platform GPL13112 the sequencer used Platform GEO Sample GSM1173819 one biological sample Sample SRA Experiment SRX314994 one library + sequencing design Experiment SRA Run SRR921999 the raw FASTQ files Run

(IDs above are from the example study GSE47966.)

A few things worth remembering:

  • It's one-to-many at every level: one project has many samples, each sample can have several experiments, and each experiment can have several runs.
  • SRR (the run) is what you actually download — FASTQ files live at the run level.
  • You'll also see SAMN… (BioSample) — e.g. SAMN02206500 — the SRA-side name for the biological material behind a GSM. labdata reports it as a BioSample field (e.g. a column in the run table) rather than a separate class.

items.title: How labdata reaches this data
items.text:
The package talks to NCBI for you through two channels:

  • Metadata → NCBI Entrez (E-utilities). Every Series, Sample, Experiment, and Run fetches its details from Entrez on demand — building the object costs nothing; the network call happens the first time you read a field, and is cached afterward.
  • Raw FASTQ → sra-tools. download() shells out to prefetch + fasterq-dump to pull and extract the reads for each run.

Because links return real objects, you can walk the tree in plain Python:

from labdata import Series

gse = Series("GSE47966")         # GEO Series (GSE)

for experiment in gse.experiments:   # SRX level
    for run in experiment.runs:      # SRR level — the downloadable units
        print(experiment.accession, run.accession)

That's the whole idea: start at a GEO Series, follow the links down to runs, then download. The GEO Series tutorial shows it end to end.

items.title: What's not in GEO
items.text:
The structured records above (samples, platforms, experiments, runs) are only part of a study. Two things commonly live outside that metadata — don't forget them:

  • Supplementary files. The actual ready-to-analyze outputs — count matrices, peak calls, bigWig tracks, READMEs — are usually attached to the Series as supplementary files, not encoded in the metadata. They're often the most useful part. List and fetch them directly:

    gse.supplementary_files       # ['GSE47966_RAW.tar', 'GSE47966_README.txt', 'filelist.txt']
gse.supplementary_file_urls   # full https URLs you can download

  • Whatever the paper kept elsewhere. GEO doesn't capture everything. Always read the paper's "Data Availability" and "Code Availability" statements: raw or controlled-access data may sit in another repository (dbGaP, EGA, Zenodo, …), and the analysis code typically lives on GitHub — none of which a GEO record will point you to.
